CONGRANT.TITLE: Contaminant Reduction by Watershed-Scale Filtration and Modeling
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Harmful algal blooms and sargassum inundations along the South Texas Gulf Coast becomeworsened as runoffs carrie higher loads of nutrient and contaminant from rapid urbanizationand heavier rainfalls. Building on our biochar column studies demonstrating removal ofammonia and heavy metals (Preota et al., 2025), PI team proposes a deployable technologyto reduce dissolved nutrients, metal, and pesticide loads by >=30%, combining biocharfiltrations with physical/hydro-biogeochemical modeling. This project will (1) demonstratelab- and field-scale removal of nutrients and contaminants; (2) obtain site-specific sorptionand hydraulic coefficients for model input by fitting breakthrough curves in HYDRUS-1D;(3) embed parameters into Soil & Water Assessment Tool-Qual2e coupled with an externalMass Balance model (SWAT-Qual2e-MB) to define pilot column dimensions; (4) conductoutreach with regional stormwater management; and (5) train students for future waterworkforce. Field experiments with graded biochar thickness will validate hydraulics andtreatment efficiency. ML algorithms will be applied for water quality parameters analysis toidentify data gaps and improve monitoring efforts (Norwin et al., 2025). Expected projectresults include: two field-scale biochar reactors at a wetland site, an open-access nutrient andcontaminant dataset with an interactive online dashboard, an ML-based spatial risk map,three peer-reviewed papers, and a stormwater water-quality outreach network with BMPguidelines. This project will improve runoff water quality by 30% load reductions withmodel prediction verified with field monitoring. This project offers a scientific based andscalable technology, which directly advances EPA priorities for stormwater and waterquality improvement in South Texas Gulf.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Consortium of Advanced Additive Manufacturing Research and Education for Energy Related Systems (CA2REERs)
CONGRANT.SPONORG: DOE/NNSA: National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) Minority Serving Institutions (MSI) Program
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The goal of this project is to develop and sustain the DOE Consortium of Advanced Additive Manufacturing Research and Education for Energy Related Systems (DOE CA2REERs) to expose, recruit, engage and train students from underrepresented groups for a career in Advanced Manufacturing for Energy, following a collaborative approach by a team of investigators from 3 MSI institutions and 2 DOE Labs. The minority serving education institutions include: University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (90% Hispanic), University Texas San Antonio (54% Hispanic), and University of Arizona (30% minority). The DOE/NNSA labs are Oak Ridge National Lab and Los Alamos National Lab. The consortium covers minority communities at three minority serving institutions with a total student enrollment of around 100,000 (UTRGV 27,708, UTSA 32,101, and University of Arizona 44,831). The long-term vision of the consortium is to cultivate an innovation driven manufacturing education ecosystem for Energy Innovation with programs designed to recruit young talents and prepare them with solid education and real-life experiences in energy innovation and advanced manufacturing technologies. Upon graduation, students are ready for a dream career in DOE/NNSA labs and energy industries.

Training, Research, and Education in Soil Science (TRESS)
CONGRANT.SPONORG: USDA/NIFA Hispanic-Serving Institutions (HSI) Education Grants Program
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: In the Rio Grande Valley, agriculture is constrained by soil quality issues such as high salinity and low availability of nutrients. Decades of reductions in soil-specific course hours in modern environmental science majors have left few qualified soil scientists nationally compounded by a lack of Hispanic representation in soil science and natural resources conservation. Hence, we propose to enhance education and training and provide research experience, addressing four USDA educational need areas, preparing over 280 students for soil science careers. Our faculty will develop five courses and respective lab manuals for ‘introduction to soil science’, ‘soil physics and hydrology’, ‘soil chemistry’, ‘soil biology’, and ‘soil conservation’. Experiment-based labs will utilize state-of-the art techniques and instruments from the PDs’ research. Experiential learning also includes field excursions to promote in-depth understanding of soil genesis, soil morphology, and land use. Additionally, our new and innovative Community Engaged Scholarship & Learning Experiences program enhances students’ professional competences as they solve local agricultural, soil quality and soil health challenges. Undergraduate training include internships with local farmers in partnership with Natural Resource Conservation Service (n=16) and research internships (n=16) under the mentoring of our faculty and M.Sc. students. Graduate students (n=4) will engage in mentoring and education activities within their field of research. Altogether, these activities will result in increased student retention; capacity building and training; leadership skills; and UTRGV graduates qualified for soil science careers, including USDA-NRCS Soil Conservationist positions.

The Development of an Industrial Assessment Center for South Texas
CONGRANT.SPONORG: Department of Energy (DOE), Office of Energy Efficiency & Renewable Energy (EERE)
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The four counties in deep south Texas known as the Rio Grande Valley are home to one of the fastest growing populations and one of the fastest growing manufacturing sectors in the state of Texas and world. The region is known as the Rio Grande Valley because it is located on the northern banks of the Rio Grande River which serves as the international boundary between the United States and Mexico. The Rio Grande Valley is also home to the second largest federally certified Hispanic Serving Institution (HSI) of higher education in the United States, the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV). Approximately 90% of the more than 25,000 UTRGV students are Hispanic.
The UTRGV College of Engineering and Computer Science (CECS) has been recognized for the quality of its academic programs and the numerous partnerships and collaborations that its faculty have established with more than 100 entities in its service area including manufacturers, local governments, economic development councils, two year institutions of higher education and not-for-profit organizations. The undergraduate degrees that the CECS awards in civil engineering, mechanical engineering, electrical engineering, manufacturing / industrial engineering and computer science engineering are all accredited by the Accreditation Board for Engineering and Technology (ABET).
There is a tremendous need for the creation of the South Texas Industrial Assessment Center (South Texas IAC). In spite of the Rio Grande Valley’s rapidly growing population and the growing manufacturing sector the closest Industrial Assessment Center (IAC) to deep south Texas is 350 miles away. The development of the South Texas IAC will provide industrial energy assessments to small and medium sized enterprises (SMEs) that previously did not have access to such no-cost energy assessments. Through the provision of these industrial energy assessments the South Texas IAC has the potential of assisting manufacturers to save millions of dollars each year in energy and water management costs.
The proposal to develop a South Texas Industrial Assessment Center (South Texas IAC) described herein is made possible because of a number of CECS engineering faculty who possess the requisite expertise and willingness to work with 20 UTRGV engineering students to carry out twenty industrial assessments per year. The faculty participating in the activities being proposed herein represent all of the departments in the CECS including electrical engineering, manufacturing and industrial engineering, civil engineering, and mechanical engineering. The diversity of faculty members’ areas of specialization and their various departmental affiliations in the CECS will provide students with an appreciation of the cross disciplinary nature of industrial energy assessments. The diversity of faculty will also ensure that engineering students throughout the CECS will become aware of the existence of the South Texas IAC and will have the opportunity to participate in the assessment activities as well as internships and research projects that come about as a result of the creation of the South Texas IAC.
As manufacturing enterprises in the Rio Grande Valley become aware of the tremendous financial benefits that accrue to them from the energy assessments offered through the South Texas IAC it is anticipated that small and large manufacturers alike will contribute to the financial viability of the South Texas IAC after grant funds expire.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Planning Grant: Engineering Research Center for Water Conservation/Management among Energy Industry, Agriculture, and Municipality
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The proposed ERC vision will be to develop a complete infrastructure for water conservation and management among energy industry, agriculture, and municipalities. There will be detailed water analysis on produced water and fracture fluid return from energy industry, water runoff from agriculture use, and greywater from municipality. The analysis will be summarized into a matrix that groups similar quality water products in order to generate a better perspective and overview of various water supplies. The next phase will be to employ various treatment strategies and determine the resulting water quality. These data will also be summarized in order to get a better perspective on achievements of each treatment technique. Based on literature review and detailed study on quality of water required for various applications (energy industry including petroleum (oil and gas), geothermal, agriculture, and municipality), a selection matrix will be developed on how the treated water can be utilized. A detailed study on the proximity of various industries will be conducted throughout the nation with emphasis on areas with greater density of oil and gas industry and agriculture. This analysis will indicate most optimal locations for synergy among the various stakeholders with greatest economical and societal impact. The impact of this water conservation/management on reduction of water disposal sites with possible contamination and seismic activities will be studied. In addition, the project will determine if there is a need to develop new technology or to combine existing treatment strategies in a new manner in order to achieve the required water quality given the influent water quality. Based on that determination, there might be work on developing those new methods to achieve the required objective. Furthermore, the quantity of water that can be conserved/managed among the various sectors nationwide will be determined, as that will measure the impact of this collaborative effort.

CONGRANT.TITLE: A Novel X-ray System to Enhance Research and Education on Structural, Medical and Nanostructured Materials at Rio Grande Valley, Texas
Exploratory Investigation on Multiphase Oscillating Flow and Heat Transfer in Engineered Porous Media of Thermoacoustic Atmospheric Water Generator
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The significant growth of population, deteriorating environment and climate change have led to increased need for freshwater. Nevertheless, water is still a limited resource to most of the arid and rural areas. The Thermoacoustic Atmospheric Water Generator (TAAWG) can condense water vapor on the surface of its regenerator (porous media), therefore it can provide a reliable and easily-accessible water supply to people under aforementioned conditions. CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The significant growth of population, deteriorating environment and climate change have led to increased need for freshwater. Nevertheless, water is still limited resource to most of arid and rural areas, it can also be considered scarce in urban areas when natural disasters happen (e.g. hurricane or earthquake). The Thermoacoustic Atmospheric Water Generator (TAAWG) can condense water vapor on the surface of its regenerator (porous media), therefore it can provide a reliable and easily-accessible water supply to people under aforementioned conditions. However, due to the complicated transport phenomenon involved, the multiphase oscillating flow and heat transfer in porous media remain poorly understood and analytically intractable. Furthermore, it is extremely difficult to carry out velocity and temperature measurements inside the porous media. Finally, to create desired porous media with a low thermal conductity which is required to maintain a temperature gradient in regenrator, suitable fabircation processes is needed, and special coating on the surface of engineered porous media is also required. Therefore, to better understand the fundamentals of thermal-fluid performance of engineered porous structure, the interdisciplinary team, combining experts in multiphase heat transfer, advanced manufacturing and non-destructive testing/imaging, will tackle both fundamental issues and technical challenges in the realization of the atmospheric water generator.

PRESENT.TITLE: Corn stover, Orange peel, and pistachio shell biochars as a filter media for removing lead and arsenic in water
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: The main threats to human health from heavy metals are associated with exposure to lead, cadmium, mercury and arsenic. This study evaluated three different biochars pyrolyzed with locally-sourced feedstock materials in South Texas as a filter media for removing lead (Pb) and arsenic (As) in water. Biochar is a highly porous charcoal produced by the combustion of biomass with limited or no oxygen (pyrolysis). Although biochar has been used as a soil amendment for a long time, the idea of using other feedstocks (e.g. plant biomass, manure, biosolids) to make biochars for water treatment is relatively new. The objective of this study is to 1) produce biochar from locally sourced feedstocks, corn stover (CS), orange peel (OP), and pistachio shell (PS), and 2) evaluate the biochar’s physico-chemical properties (pH, surface area, electrical conductivity, elemental composition, Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy, and Scanning electron microscopy with energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy). Feedstock materials were pyrolyzed under nitrogen conditions at temperature (300, 450, or 600°C). Our results showed that higher pyrolysis temperature resulted in higher surface areas for PS and CS biochars, which likely enhanced the adsorbent potential for lead (Pb). The optimal pH was found to be 6 for all biochar types in the solution pH range between 2 and 6 with percent Pb removal being 96% for CS, 95% for OP, and 19% for PS biochar. Biochars without surface modification was not effective in removing arsenic in water. Magnetized biochar was produced to evaluate its adsorbent properties for the arsenic removal in aqueous solution. Isotherm and pH studies were done to show the effectiveness of magnetic biochar in removing As (III) and As (V).

PRESENT.ABSTRACT: Biochar is a highly porous charcoal produced by the combustion of biomass with limited or no oxygen. Biochar is viewed as an approach to carbon sequestration as much of the carbon in it is fixed into a recalcitrant form while improving soil structure in the long-term. There is also an increasing interest to use biochars for environmental remediation. While most of previous studies have focused on applications for wastewater treatment, there are limited studies on stormwater treatment. Stormwater in urban areas passes the impervious ground surfaces and carries pathogen, suspended solids, nutrients, heavy metals, and organic chemicals. To improve the effluent quality and harvest stormwater for non-potable use, bioretention and other means of low impact development have attracted many interests. Biochar can be a promising filter media due to its high adsorption capacity. This project aims to evaluate plant-derived biochars as a filter media for stormwater treatment. Contaminants of interest are nutrients (phosphate and nitrate) and heavy metals (copper, lead, and zinc). Three different biochar materials (oak tree, wheat straw, and wood biochars) will be compared to a commercial activated carbon as filter materials. Preliminary results from batch adsorption experiments using the four filter materials and their characterization by X-ray micro computed topography will be presented in context of their potential for stormwater treatment.

PRESENT.TITLE: Removal of heavy metals and nutrients using charcoal-based adsorbents
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: Urban stormwater runoff is often contaminated by heavy metals and nutrients as it washes through different impervious surfaces. Contaminants in stormwater runoff can be treated by various conventional physicochemical techniques (e.g., chemical precipitation, ion exchange, eletrodialysis, and reverse osmosis). However, most of these methods are either economically unfavorable, technically complicated, or spatially too limited. In urban settings, it is often difficult to provide an area that is adequate to have detention storage pond. Therefore, the use of a filtration system has received greater attention to remove contaminants within a smaller space. The purpose of this study is to compare different types of relatively low-cost charcoal-derived adsorbents to remove stormwater contaminants: commercial activated carbon, oak tree biochar, wood biochar, and wheat straw biochar. Contaminates in interest were heavy metals (Zn, Cr, and Cu) and nutrients (NO3-N, PO4-P). Kinetics study and batch adsorption experiments using the four different materials will be presented for individual contaminants.

SEED FUNDING: SUBMISSION, AWARD, IMPLEMENTATION and IMPACT

An important strategy to attain higher education research impact is to promote collaboration among university investigators. One effective mechanism to achieve this synergy is through seed funding for collaborative research.
Selected faculty will discuss the seed grant submission process, administration of funds, project management inclusive of co-leadership and engagement. Other possible topics to be discussed are identifying potential problems, how they were addressed, and how seed grants potentially assist with applying for external funds.
